output.title: What staged delivery hides in a small-business workflow
output.body:
Staged delivery hides a practical decision: do you keep doing a recurring task by hand, hire for it, or test a bounded automation first?

When you break automation into a pilot MVP and then expansion, the useful part is what gets revealed early. A good diagnostic should identify one recurring workflow, say honestly whether AI fits, and, if it does, define the pilot scope, fixed price, and measures before anyone talks about scaling. That is less dramatic than a big roadmap. It is also more useful.

Bareni’s normal sequence is straightforward: a free diagnostic, a fixed-price pilot in weeks, then expansion or an optional retainer. Those timings are intended scopes, not guarantees. Bareni also offers a separate AI Strategy & Roadmap for owners who want strategy only, so this is about sequencing the work, not pretending roadmaps are useless.

The control matters too. Finished code is handed over, and the database, automation-tool, and API accounts stay in the customer’s name from the start. That is Bareni’s no-lock-in policy, not a legal warranty. Human approval stays in place for money movement and other high-risk decisions.

If you are deciding where to start, name one frequent, repeatable workflow with a measurable outcome — customer emails, invoices, or lead logging are obvious examples. That is the first thing to test, before you start drawing the nice-looking arrows.
